content.thinking:
I need to write the postmortem without stating any raw figures directly, instead using placeholder labels like {A1}, {A2} wherever a number, time, percentage, or commit hash would appear, and referring to deploys by labels like P2 rather than hashes.

Working out the causal chain: the symptom is shopper totals not reconciling, traced to record_purchase no longer maintaining the running total after a specific deploy, with onset timing matching that deploy closely — though I note this remains the leading unconfirmed candidate since no logs were actually reviewed. I'm also noting contributing factors like the periodic nature of the integrity check, lack of test coverage, rollback only being recommended rather than automated, and the need for a backfill of existing records — each becoming a new action item (AI-3 through AI-5), alongside the open rollback item (AI-2) and the draft fix (AI-1), while being careful to phrase timing details like "periodic check" without spelling out the actual interval.

action_items.item: Run the spend-integrity check far more often, for example after each deploy and on a short schedule, and page when any total diverges from its purchases. Do not wait for the periodic run.
Add a test, run before release, that records purchases and asserts the account's total_this_month_cents equals the sum of its purchases. Require it to pass for any change to record_purchase.
Recompute total_this_month_cents for every affected shopper from their purchase history. Verify with the integrity check that all totals reconcile, and record the result.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' stored spend totals did not match the purchases behind them. The check found {A1} of {A2} totals wrong, the widest short by {A3}, with the oldest affected purchase at {A4}. The service stayed available and produced no errors.
New purchases were being recorded without the account's monthly total (total_this_month_cents) being updated, so each purchase widened the gap between the stored total and the real purchases.

The release deployed at the start of the affected period changed record_purchase in purchase_ledger.py so it no longer maintains that total. The onset placed by Argus matches the deploy time. The earlier deploy was hours before and does not line up with the onset.

The change reached production and stayed there unnoticed. No metric moved, and the only thing that saw the wrong totals was the periodic reconciliation check. That check had no earlier run to catch the drift sooner. The evidence stops here: no logs or code diff were read, so why the change dropped the maintained total is not established.

contributing_factors.factor: The reconciliation check runs only periodically ({A5}), so data corruption with no latency or error signal could go undetected for up to that long. The fault ran from {began} until the alert at {alert_raised}.
Nothing in review or testing caught that record_purchase no longer maintained the monthly total. No test or pre-release check ties the stored total to the purchases behind it.
Rollback was not taken automatically, because nothing would show within Argus's waiting time whether it worked. It was left for a person and was still open, so the drift could continue.
Rolling back or fixing the code does not repair totals already written. Those records need their own rewrite, and nothing in the record covers it.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers' monthly spend totals stopped matching their actual purchases. A periodic integrity check found that {A1} of {A2} shopper totals were wrong, the widest by {A3}. The fault began at {began}, shortly after a code release, and had not been fixed when the last metrics were read. So it lasted at least {duration}, and that figure is a lower bound. The service stayed fast and error-free, so no ordinary alert fired. Only the periodic check ({A5}) caught it. Argus investigated, pointed to the release as the likely cause, and proposed a code fix as a draft pull request. It did not roll back on its own, because nothing would have shown inside its waiting time whether the rollback worked. It left the rollback for a person. Rolling back stops further drift but does not repair the totals already written, which need a separate rewrite.

got_lucky: The wrong totals did not cause errors or visible outages, but shoppers could still have seen incorrect totals for the whole period. The integrity check happened to catch it; without it the drift would have continued.
went_well: Argus picked up the alert at once, placed the onset at the deploy time and named the release as the leading candidate.
Argus did not take a rollback it could not verify, and recommended it instead.
A draft fix pull request was proposed within moments of the alert.
went_wrong: The fault went undetected for a long time because only a periodic check could see it. Latency and error metrics showed nothing.
No metrics from before the onset were available, so no error-rate baseline could be built.
No logs were read, so the cause rests on timing and inference. Both candidates were never tried.
The rollback and fix were still open at the end of the response, so the drift had not stopped.

input.root_cause: The later deploy (P2) changed record_purchase in purchase_ledger.py so it no longer maintains the account's total_this_month_cents. Every purchase recorded after the deploy left the shopper's stored total out of step with the purchases behind it. This is the leading candidate (C1, C2). No logs were read and no action was tried to confirm it.
